This paper presents an enhanced version of Canopus, a highly available consensus protocol tailored for high-performance computing environments. While Canopus enables rapid agreement on values despite node crashes, we have further optimized it to tolerate node failures while addressing Byzantine errors, while simultaneously maintaining its performance efficiency. Our improvements include a mechanism to prevent double voting and a strategy to circumvent double counting. Additionally, we have designed a method to identify and handle node failures more effectively. Evaluation demonstrates that our new protocol, named RCanopus, achieves a 20% improvement in agreement speed compared to Canopus and provides robust protection against Byzantine errors, provided that less than one-third of the nodes are malicious.

Lateral lipid segregation and liquid-ordered domains within the bilayer are crucial for numerous cellular functions, a property largely driven by cholesterol. To better grasp how cholesterol influences membrane elasticity, we conducted bending modulus measurements on a multi-component system featuring cholesterol using an optical method. This approach involves tracking changes in the curvature-dependent surface polarizance of a membrane under applied bending forces. Our findings indicate that cholesterol enhances the bilayer's rigidity, revealing a progressive stiffening of a multi-component bilayer saturated with approximately 35% cholesterol up to roughly 10 times its initial modulus. This progression mirrors the emergence of liquid-ordered phases and aligns with previous nuclear magnetic resonance data. The optical technique offers a highly sensitive means to evaluate the rigidity of lipid membranes containing cholesterol.

We present a loop quantum gravitational framework derived from the Ashtini-Maebari Hamilton. This model features an additional parameter, $\lambda$, which modifies the Holst action. Analyzing the corresponding Hamiltonian dynamics, we identify that the theory converges to general relativity when $\lambda$ equals zero, aligning with general relative conditions. By applying Hamiltonian isolation techniques, we obtain the Beinfeld-Mass formula for the primary model variation. Through the separation process using isolation variables, the dynamics are expressed in terms of Beinfeld-Mass variables, allowing for an explicit quantization procedure. The resulting quantum operator is defined as the Thaf-Neyl-Adhtasi-Bernard Hamilton, which exhibits significant progress in loop gravity theory. By utilizing holonomic variables, the operator is expressed in an action form, enabling a clear separation between Beinfeld-Mass terms and other components. This allows for an explicit separation of the Beinfeld-Mass terms, leading to an explicit quantization of the Beinfeld-Mass operator. The resulting Beinfeld-Mass matrix is then used to calculate the Beinfeld-Mass spectrum, which provides valuable insights into the Beinfeld-Mass physics.

The Pierre Auger Observatory, as the largest instrument dedicated to detecting the highest-energy cosmic rays, has recorded several particles exceeding an energy threshold of 10^19 eV. The comprehensive dataset compiled during its Phase I operational period is now made available through an open-access online registry. This document provides a detailed description of the comprehensive registry and its key attributes. The registry's primary utility lies in facilitating comprehensive searches for extensive air shower events, even those lacking sufficient energy for publication, thereby supporting future comprehensive studies of the entire catalog.

Recent advancements in deep object detection have produced models that achieve remarkable accuracy, yet their lack of interpretability and inability to quantify uncertainty are critical barriers to practical application. This study introduces a straightforward and effective approach to assessing uncertainty in object detectors. By treating the inference stage of a detector as an inference process for the target parameters of a Bayesian model, the method allows for uncertainty estimation through Monte Carlo Dropout within frameworks like Fast R-CNN and RetinaNet across various datasets. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed technique yields competitive uncertainty assessments compared to current state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, outperforming contemporary approaches by 10%, the method significantly boosts confidence in high-quality predictions while suppressing uncertainty for low-confidence ones.

Accurate traffic prediction is vital for enhancing transportation infrastructure and minimizing congestion. While existing methods often rely on historical data from expansive networks, they frequently fail to account for the granular details of current traffic states. This approach is particularly problematic when dealing with congested conditions or novel events, such as new construction projects. This paper introduces a novel framework for predicting future traffic states by focusing on recent "traffic flowing snippets" (TFSs). A TFS is a sequence of road segments that share consistent flow patterns. By analyzing the evolution of these snippets over time, the framework captures fine-grained dynamics to forecast future states. The proposed system employs a neural network to model both spatial and temporal dependencies within TFSs, enabling the system to anticipate future traffic states. The model's efficacy was validated using two real-world datasets, demonstrating significant performance gains over current state-of-the-art methods.

Precise quantification of hippocampal gray matter (GM) and white matter (WM) volumes is critical for investigating the progression of neurological illnesses, particularly those affecting the hippocampus, such as epilepsy and Alzheimer's. This study introduces an advanced automatic segmentation framework for these brain regions, validated across an extensive dataset comprising 1,100 T1 MRI scans from patients with epilepsy, Alzheimer's, or healthy controls. The framework utilizes numerous convolutional neural (CNN) architectures to generate robust segmentation outcomes. Specifically, it employs a three-step strategy: first, a UNet architecture delineates the full hippocampus; second, specialized 3D CNN models separate distinct sub-regions of the hippocampus; third, additional 3D CNN models partition the hippocampal GM and WM. The proposed methods were rigorously evaluated using various metrics, including the Dice coefficient, Jaccard index, and the 90th percentile Hausdorff distance. Performance assessments included statistical comparisons against other deep learning approaches and traditional atlased methods. The study further examines the efficacy of these segmentation tools in detecting hippocampal abnormalities associated with epilepsy and age-related atrophy typically found in Alzheimer's patients.

Although Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are widely favored for processing graph data, they typically face challenges with graph generation, hyperparameter tuning, and the absence of theoretical foundations. We present a universal pGNN architecture capable of handling graph data through a hierarchy of pyramid-like shrinkage skeletons. Within this framework, we propose two specific sub-models utilizing the shrinkage approach to resolve issues regarding input graph generation and network parameter optimization. In response to the limitation of current GNNs in retaining structural information, our proposed sub-models employ a universal, theoretical, and hierarchical method to enhance their topology-awareness. The Framework known as Astrodust+PAH (FP) serves as a unified, self-consistent, and predictive photoelectric model of the diffuse interstellar medium (DISM). It offers a comprehensive description of dust extinction, emission, and polarization, while simultaneously quantifying dust properties and deriving mechanisms for light polarization. The core architecture relies on a size-temperature distribution of silicate grains and the hydrogen/acetylene-based PAHs. The temperature of these silicates is governed by the photoelectric effect, which also allows the distribution to function as a precise "dust cooling thermostat." In this model, silicate extinction is treated as a size-based distribution, and silicate emission arises from vibration-rotation transitions among excited states. The current iteration of the model utilizes the "dust sphere approximation," which accounts for polarization by modeling dust as an ellipsoid and light scattering via an atomic cluster. This configuration enables the derivation of the size-to-ellipticity relation and the hydrogen-to-carbon ratio in PAHs from observed data. Consequently, the model predicts that in the diffuse interstellar medium, silicates possess an aspect ratio of 0.96 and the hydrogen-to-carbon ratio in PAHs is 1.9, aligning well with recent observational findings.

The discovery of CIDA 1 b, a massive exoplanet orbiting an extremely low-mass star (ELM), is significant. Its host star, CIDA 1, has a mass of 0.079 M_sun, which is the lowest recorded for a confirmed planet host. This system features a gas giant with a mass of 1.6 M Jup situated at 0.03 AU, a separation consistent with a tidal-capture scenario. Leveraging ALMA observations, we have identified a distinct gap in the system's circumstellar disk, which we attribute to the planet's tidal capture. This gap is the first evidence indicating that disk structures can form even around ELMs. Additionally, our data suggest that the system's outer edge, located at 11.6 AU, is the result of gas accretion ceasing at the snow line. This finding highlights a critical insight for understanding the formation of planets in ELM systems.

Abstract Interpretation (AI) is a technique used to formally verify program properties, but its computational cost is often prohibitive. This paper introduces a method to reduce the complexity of specific sub-programs within a given global fixed point by utilizing an "unknown" variable to decouple their rising and falling phases. This decoupling process involves a computation-intensive operation performed only once during initialization, followed by significantly cheaper updates in subsequent steps. The decoupling algorithm is validated on both C and Java programs to demonstrate a reduction in both time and space complexity. The results indicate that the time performance of this decoupling approach is equivalent to that of standard fixed-point computation during the AI's rising phase.

Controlling lattice distortions in multiferroics is essential for manipulating their magnetic and ferroelectric characteristics. While geometric and dynamical multiferroicity are well-established mechanisms, geometric multiferroicity—where lattice dynamics generate chirality-induced magnetization—remains underutilized. This study reveals that photo-induced lattice deformations in the perovskite bismuth ferrite ($\text{FeBiO}_3$) exhibit geometric magnetization comparable in magnitude to that produced by dynamical means. Density Functional Theory calculations demonstrate that ultrafast optical excitation triggers ferroelectric domain wall motion, thereby generating spin polarization. These findings establish light as a viable tool for activating geometric magnetization within multiferroics, offering new avenues for tuning spin and magnetic properties through lattice manipulation.

Data anomalies can severely impact the integrity of machine learning models and data-driven systems. Although various anomaly detection methods exist, most are limited to specific data types, such as numerical or categorical. This study introduces a universal approach applicable to arbitrary metric spaces. The method constructs an anomaly flag for every data point by evaluating its overall closeness to others; it then identifies out-of-distribution instances as those falling beyond a defined threshold. This approach is non-parametric and non-parametric and does not require predefined assumptions about the data. The graph-based closeness metric enables efficient processing of large datasets, and the threshold can be automatically calibrated using unsupervised techniques. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world data demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm.

An atom positioned near a thin reflective surface experiences a self-force and a corresponding self-emission resulting from its coupling to the van der Waals forces of the mirror. This study investigates additional stimulation and emission induced by the mirror's motion parallel to the atom-mirror gap. We derive a precise analytical expression for this effect and compare it with the scenario of a moving source coupled to a standard electromagnetic mode. It is demonstrated that the parameters of atomic excitation and the resulting emission can be fine-tuned by adjusting three key variables: the mirror-missing distance, its shape, and its velocity. These findings suggest a novel method for controlling the atomic states of an individual, well-resolved emitter using a mirror that is both thin and sharp.

Graph neural networks (GNNs) are widely used across various domains, driven by their ability to effectively handle diverse graph structures. However, recent studies indicate that GNNs can be easily misled by adversarial attacks, which undermine their practical application. To address this, we introduce the Localized Community Equity (LCE) metric, designed to measure community-based equity within graphs. This metric effectively identifies regions contributing the most to GNN prediction errors. By analyzing these LCE-highlighted areas, we demonstrate that these attack-critical regions often contain higher adversarial equity than attack-critical but low-LCE regions. Consequently, the LCE metric facilitates GNN debugging, enabling researchers to better comprehend model failures in response to specific attacks. This deeper insight paves the way for developing more robust and reliable graph machine learning models.

This study proposes a novel algorithm to estimate the kinetic rate constants ($k_i$) for reversible enzymatic processes starting from noisy single-molecule time-lapse fluorescence data. The method iteratively solves the corresponding reversible kinetic equations to solve for the time-dependent probability density, $p(\mathbf{x}, t)$, by minimizing the discrepancy between the simulated fluorescence FCS autocorrelation function (FCS) and the experimental dataset. Specifically, $p(\mathbf{x}, t)$ is obtained as a solution to the Fokker-Planck equation (FPE) associated with a Krams-Chitwood (Kramers) diffusion process. Utilizing the conjugate gradient method to minimize a FCS-based objective function yields the optimal $p(\mathbf{x}, t)$ for a given set of $k_i$ parameters. Subsequently, an optimization routine adjusts the $k_i$ values to further minimize the error between observed and predicted FCS curves, yielding the final set of kinetic constants. This research presents a "Levers and Swells" framework to model financial crises, which is a fundamental component of our broader "Levers, Swells, and Switches" theory of crisis dynamics. The framework integrates two distinct mechanisms: a "flood of funds" model, representing a stochastic mean-reverting duration with random termination, and a "leverage" model, defined as the Meir-Kaloumnikoff log-expected-value function. The authors introduce two statistical tests designed to identify the termination events in mean-reverting processes and estimate their probabilities of occurrence. Additionally, the study offers a non-parametric algorithm for calculating $E[x]$ that remains robust against heavy-tailed distributions. Empirical analysis applies these levers and flood models to global financial swells, utilizing "logical expectation" financial swell metrics derived from Levers' theory. The estimated parameters for each swell's lever are provided, and the validity of the probabilistic termination assumptions is verified through the statistical testing of the log-expected-value levers.

This study examines the quantum harmonic oscillator under a constant force $F$ by employing the path integral formalism, where the corresponding Euclidean quantum operator is constructed. A domain of $[0,\beta]$ is established to perform Monte Carlo simulations of both open and closed configurations. Within these frameworks, the partition functions are computed, and subsequent differentiation of the open-system partition function with respect to $\beta$ yields the ground-state energy. Specifically, energies derived from closed-loop simulations are contrasted with those from open configurations. Furthermore, employing parallel tempering to mitigate autocorrelation, convergence regarding the free energy is demonstrated. Finally, the efficacy of the open-system approach is highlighted, showing that it can accurately calculate ground-state energy, thereby validating its reliability.

Item recommendation, a prevalent technique in online retail, aims to suggest relevant products to users by leveraging their historical purchase or rating data. While traditional methods, such as collaborative filtering (CF), struggle with scalability and cold-start challenges, item-based recommendation approaches have emerged as a competitive alternative. However, these approaches often struggle to effectively capture the nuanced relationships between different items. To address this, this study introduces a novel framework that utilizes embedding techniques to represent latent features of items and transform user-item interactions into sentence representations. These sentences are then input into a neural network to generate prediction scores. To enhance model efficacy, attention mechanisms are employed to refine sentence encoding, and item embeddings are optimized using contrastive contrastive loss contrasting similar and dissimilar items. Notably, our model surpasses existing models by incorporating sentiment information, which aids in disentangling positive and negative signals within user ratings. Empirical evaluations across three real-world datasets confirm the proposed method's superior performance, achieving significant improvements over state-of-the-art baselines.

This study introduces a novel approach to enhancing Arabic-English code-switched learning by leveraging lexical substitutions. It presents a new task focused on identifying these substitutions within Italian data. A model is constructed to handle this task, and its utility in expanding lexical knowledge for Arabic-English switching users is analyzed. The results demonstrate that lexical substitutions serve as a valuable resource, facilitating improved performance in lexical acquisition and enhancing accuracy in machine translation.

Current methods for identifying novel entity relationships primarily depend on inner product operations, such as the dot product, which integrate entity and relation embeddings to compute scores. These approaches are heavily influenced by the scale of the existing knowledge graph and frequently result in score vanishing. To mitigate these challenges, this paper presents a connection prediction-driven approach for entity relationship exploration. By leveraging predictions made during knowledge graph completion, the method aims to identify relationships that are more informative and less prone to vanishing scores. Additionally, a novel VGG-style neural network architecture is introduced to combine quaternions—representations of two complex embeddings—to calculate relationship scores. Empirical results demonstrate the method's superior performance compared to state-of-the-art baselines, particularly in addressing the issues of vanishing scores and image similarity.

The simulation of analog-to-digital converters (ADCs) in SPICE, while complex, can be effectively achieved by incorporating an equivalent behavioral model. This study presents the development of such an ADC model designed to replicate the nonlinear switching latency of ADCs, which is often significant when simulating high-speed systems. This analytical approach, which utilizes the "Curve Fitting Toolbox" to fit SPICE subcircuit data, provides a space-efficient and scalable solution. It enables the accurate and efficient simulation of ADCs with up to 12-bit resolution and sampling frequencies reaching up to 100 MHz.

This work examines the rough-grained smoothness condition, recently proposed by Liang et al. (2021) for Reinforcement Learning with noisy feedback, and extends it to both deterministic and stochastic metric spaces. Under this assumption, which unifies concepts like bounded smoothness and bounded adversarial sensitivity, the convergence rates of Perturbation-based Policy Optimization (PPO) for black-box reinforcement learning improve significantly in terms of sample complexity. Notably, the analysis covers rough-grained smoothness within rough gradients as the core framework. When integrated with the findings of (Liu, 2020), the paper establishes an accelerated convergence rate for the adversarially bandit linear setting, effectively resolving an open issue from that work.

Although animacy is understood to be a fundamental capability crucial for processing natural vision, its specific neural mechanisms remain unclear. This study investigates the ontogeny of animacy in human visual cortex using a "Natural Images Dataset" (NID) comprising face, object, and scene categories. The research reveals that source free from pre-training exhibits strong animacy-related representations across the entire visual stream. Furthermore, representations associated with animacy emerge in the early visual areas of the NID even in untrained conditions. The findings suggest that animacy representations are innate to the visual system and precede the development of higher-level category expertise. These results underscore the significance of animacy in human visual development and highlight a foundational role alongside other innate features like biological motion.

Accurately simulating dynamic processes, such as those in manufacturing, relies heavily on the fidelity of finite element method (FEM) results. Since numerical errors are inevitable, this research introduces a novel filtering technique designed to enhance the accuracy of finite element simulations. The filter's implementation details and underlying algorithm are described, followed by an evaluation of its efficacy. Comparative analysis against the standard Kriging metamodeling approach demonstrates the proposed method's superior performance.

The corona of black hole binaries is a critical area of inquiry, as its structure and composition are pivotal to understanding the accretion process and the nature of X-ray emissions. This study investigates the corona's evolution during outbursts in the black hole system MAXI J1535-571, specifically examining Type-C quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) known as "corona-like QPOs" (CLMs), using data from the Insight-HXMT mission. We tracked the CLM frequency and the corresponding X-ray spectral properties throughout the outburst. Our findings indicate that the QPO frequencies remained constant at approximately 1.2 Hz during hard, soft, and flat spectral states. Furthermore, spectral analysis reveals that the corona's temperature and the broadening of the iron K$\alpha$ emission line vary inversely with the spectral hardness. Consequently, the source of X-rays in this system is determined to be composite, arising from both a hot corona and a geometrically thick disk.

To acquire the ability to adapt to non-deterministic environments, agents must first possess the capacity to detect and respond appropriately to the actions of their surroundings, including other agents. In the context of social reinforcement learning, this capability is vital for enabling transfer learning and effectively cooperating with associated agents who also exhibit their own motivational drivers. This paper introduces a novel, inherent mechanism for "Transfer Enable" into the social motivation framework, ensuring that agents' experiences are optimized to benefit their associates. The efficacy of this approach in dynamic agents who react unpredictably and unpredictably is demonstrated through experiments involving both predictable and unpredictable agents.

We present a new contrastive learning technique designed for substance identification, which integrates physics-based models with data and leverages the physics knowledge to enhance learning efficiency. By applying the physics-awareness to visualize the feature embedding space, the approach enables the identification of unknown materials in untrained areas of the spectrum and physical parameters using minimal labeled examples. We have tested this framework using high-resolution X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) spectra from binary mixtures of $\text{CeO}_2$ and $\text{CeO}_{2-x}$, achieving excellent agreement with ground-truth compositions. Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that incorporating physics-based models significantly improves the effectiveness of contrastive learning in experimental settings.

This article provides a thorough and organized examination of Lie 2-groups, with emphasis on their standard models. It is structured into two sections: the first explores Lie 2-theories arising from group extensions and 2-theories linked to crossed modules, while the second covers 2-theories associated with Lie 2-groups and their corresponding Lie algebra 2-groups. We also provide connections to higher Lie theory, n-Lie groups, and higher crossed modules throughout.

Recent breakthroughs in image feature point detectors and matchers, as well in descriptor generation, have driven significant performance gains in visual feature matching. Nevertheless, these parametric methods face limitations regarding their domain specificity and sensitivity to domain shifts, primarily because their fixed-step architectures rely on domain-dependent hyperparameters tuned for distinct task types, such as detecting corners versus handling self-overlapping regions. To address this, we introduce a novel non-parametric approach, LoFTR (Local feature Transformer-RoI), which relies solely on image input and requires no pre-trained model weights. Utilizing a unified transformer-based architecture, LoFTR simultaneously generates keypoint matches without needing separate modules for detectors or matchers, thereby offering a flexible solution adaptable to diverse tasks through straightforward parameter initialization rather than relying on fixed, task-specific components. Furthermore, we have established a new benchmark, the SUN-Robot dataset, featuring 1,200 real-world image pairs collected from outdoor environments, specifically optimized to evaluate matching performance in challenging conditions like low textures. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that LoFTR consistently outperforms current non-parametric methods and rivals the accuracy of state-of-the-art parametric systems.

Accurate data on solar vector magnetic fields are essential for investigating the mechanisms behind this field generation and subsequent evolution. Existing studies indicate that measurement biases in these vectors stem from the physical limitations inherent in the observation process. This study presents a new, model-independent framework for identifying such biases across all magnetic field components. Using this model to analyze data from the Solar Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HSMI) on the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO), we pinpoint specific biases affecting polarization measurements. To mitigate issues arising from the bias in the $Q$ and $U$ polarization signals, a novel, non-linear, non-parametric inversion technique has been developed. This method accounts for both varying precision and systematic errors in the observed polarization. Comparative analysis with the standard "minimum variance" inversion used in HDI data processing reveals that the proposed inversion approach yields significantly improved accuracy in horizontal field measurements near the solar limb.

This study examines the Rastall theory to derive the first complete set of static, charged black hole solutions characterized by spherical symmetry. These solutions are defined within a $(3+1)$-dimensional framework, where the spacetime geometry is described by the Einstein-Rosen metric. The validity of this model is contingent upon the Rastall theory satisfying its fundamental postulate. Utilizing the Hawking emission formula, the paper calculates the specific emission rates for charged black holes under this theory. The derived formulas demonstrate dependence on the charge $Q$, Rastall parameter $\lambda$, and mass $M$. Furthermore, the influence of gravity on the emission dynamics under consideration is analyzed. The study also explores the conditions for the existence of these black holes, specifically focusing on their event horizons and singular points. Theoretical and numerical results are presented to illustrate the complex relationship between Rastall parameters, mass, and charge in the context of Hawking emission mechanisms.

This work investigates two metrics: spectral distance and distortion, which are used to quantify the rate of convergence in Von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem. These metrics are complete, separable spaces that are Polish, making them suitable candidates for probability. By defining specific probability measures on this space, the field of study expands to include characteristic distributions. Furthermore, these distributions are demonstrated to correspond exactly to free random variables associated with the identity element in unital $C^*$-algebra. In the context of $C^*$-factors, concepts of entropy are explored, with computational methods derived for specific finite-dimensional examples. Finally, these finite-dimensional cases are analyzed regarding their convergence speeds within Von Neumann's theorem.

The Gaia Blue-Pasband (BP) and Red-Pasband (RP) spectra are powerful tools for identifying stars with low metallicity, a process essential for mapping the chemical evolution of the Galaxy and its satellite systems. This study presents the development of a methodology to detect metal-poor stars using these specific data sets. We define a "metallicity index" by combining RP and BP data, which, when compared against the original selection criteria, demonstrates an improved ability to select metal-poor stars. Applying this refined technique to the open clusters NGC 6791, M92, and M68, we derived metallicity estimates of $[M/H] = -0.36 \pm 0.03$, $-0.19 \pm 0.03$, and $-0.21 \pm 0.03$, respectively. These values align well with existing literature values for these clusters when corrected for distance and reddening.

This study investigates which aspects of language are captured by corpus-based metrics of morphological complexity, focusing on the interplay between morphological complexity and the linguistic factors of morph, morphosyntactic, and syntactic complexity. Drawing on a collection of 22 metrics for morphological complexity, we analyze the relationships between these indices and measures of morphosyntactic and syntactic complexity, then validate our findings through a series of authenticating experiments. Results indicate that all investigated metrics correlate significantly with both morphosyntactic and syntactic complexity. However, cross-lingue validation reveals that a morphosyntactic–morphological complexity relationship observed in English does not consistently hold across other languages. Furthermore, authenticating experiments demonstrate that while these metrics successfully differentiate between languages exhibiting varying degrees of morphological complexity, they fail to distinguish morphological complexity within a single language. Ultimately, the evidence suggests that morphological complexity metrics function as proxies for linguistic complexity overall rather than isolating the morphological domain; this finding offers a robust theoretical basis for explaining the consistent positive correlations between these metrics and morphological complexity across diverse linguistic contexts.

We approach model reduction as a learning task where an optimal policy is derived from an environment model, positing that the model itself can be learned. While partial insights into this model are available, they are insufficient to determine the exact objective. We demonstrate that coarse-grained model classes can be discovered to achieve the optimal policy without requiring the unique, exact model. Furthermore, we establish that model simplification can occur even when the insights used to guide that simplification are incorrect. Our discussion includes asymptotic convergence guarantees, incorporating input from linear quadratic regulators, Markov decision processes, and representation learning.

This article introduces the M-ar-K-Fast algorithm, which serves as a data-driven extension of the renowned FastICA independent component analysis (ICA) method. The original ICA approach is designed to handle single datasets, making it difficult to process scenarios with multiple inputs. In contrast, M-ar-K-Fast is engineered to effectively manage multiple datasets. The methodology is validated using both simulated data and the well-documented Enron email corpus. Performance evaluation reveals that this approach successfully isolates information sources, achieving superior results compared to the standard single-dataset ICA technique.

The exponential growth of geo-tagged social platforms has fueled research aimed at automatically detecting emerging topics and events from digital user-generated content. Nevertheless, current methods often struggle with a critical limitation: they fail to leverage the user's precise location information, treating spatial data as secondary or ignoring the dynamic movement patterns of individuals. Recognizing that online activity is deeply tied to physical location and movement history, this study proposes a new framework for identifying real-time, location-based event streams. The approach employs spatial-temporal event identification to pinpoint locations where transient gatherings occur, even when crowd density is low, by analyzing the dynamic transitions between areas. To achieve this, the user's trajectory is modeled as a piecewise linear curve, and event detection is formulated as an event-driven dynamic programming process. The system effectively identifies the optimal configuration of event boundaries and their associated spatial extents. Experimental results, derived from two real-world geotagged social datasets, validate the method's accuracy and real-time capabilities, demonstrating its practical application in live event monitoring.

We examine the circumstances permitting a given surface to possess a specific metric, defining this capability as met; this property is demonstrated to be equivalent for compact, boundary-free surfaces. For such closed metrics, a necessary prerequisite is that they satisfy both positive total curvature and positive the Euler characteristic. For cases involving non-empty boundaries, two additional requirements must be met by inducing the positive curvature on the interior and the positive induced curvature on the boundary. For a specific class of pathometric inputs, the existence problem is resolved affirmatively.

Alloys utilizing rare-earth elements serve as highly efficient permanent magnets, though their high cost and ecological impact necessitate the development of yttrium-substitute alternatives. This study targets a specific replacement of cobalt within the Y-Co-B system, which is renowned for delivering exceptional magnetization and magnetic interactions. We conducted a high-throughput computational screening of over 1,000 materials, commencing with a traditional database search that identified 10 candidates with the requisite stoichiometry. Subsequent refinement focused on total density of states (DOS) at the Fermi level and cohesive energy, narrowing the selection to seven viable candidates. Finally, after evaluating magnetic properties, seven YCoB stoichiometric materials were identified as possessing the necessary attributes for subsequent investigation.

This research examines risk-aware bidding strategies for display advertising with a specific focus on scenarios involving an limited advertising budget. Conventional methods typically evaluate performance using the expected value of returns while frequently disregarding the risks associated with high budget consumption. This paper introduces an adaptive risk-conscious bidder that leverages a Q-learning framework to maximize total advertising value. This new approach is designed to dynamically adjust bid amounts in response to market fluctuations and volatility, ensuring stable, high-value outcomes while adhering to both performance targets and budgetary limits. Empirical validation through extensive simulations demonstrates that the proposed method not only excels at budget management but also delivers superior total value compared to existing state-of-the-art solutions.

This study examines how quantum trajectories evolve when the underlying Wigner function exhibits negativity. We demonstrate that while the quantum force remains unaffected by the Wigner function's sign, the path's instantaneous velocity is directly influenced by local negativity. Specifically, the velocity experiences an abrupt magnitude shift upon entering a region of negative character, allowing the identification of the most negative zones by observing the peak velocity on the formed paths. This acceleration can also manifest as non-classical behaviors, such as effective "tunneling" of the guiding pilot wave across classically forbidden areas.

This study introduces a new privacy amplification method for the E91 Quantum Key Exchange protocol that avoids complex bound calculations by employing the Chernoff bound. The security analysis relies on entropy functions and functions related to matrix Horn inequalities, which can be efficiently solved using standard computational tools. The results indicate that, for specific parameter sets, this new approach achieves a higher number of secure final key bits compared to the conventional Shor-Presser-Wootters method, while the security analysis and calculation complexity remain comparable.

This work investigates the dynamics of timelike Bertrand curves, focusing on their behavior within a Pseudo-Riemannian 3-manifold of constant curvature, as determined. We derive the conditions under which a timelike curve satisfies these properties, noting that if a timelike curve satisfies the necessary conditions, it automatically exhibits the necessary characteristics. We also explore the relationship between a timelike curve and curves that share their fundamental structural features, noting that these curves must satisfy specific geometric constraints, such as those derived by considering curves that lie in the same ambient space and satisfy specific differential equations. We further analyze how these curves behave under various transformations, noting that they preserve certain key features under the action of the isometry group and satisfy specific differential equations that characterize their geometry.

We introduce combined distributions for the sum of $n$ independent, independent marginally identical (i.i.d.) Feller processes. While these sums generally fail to be marginally identical on their own, the proposed distributions address this by defining a specific probability measure over all possible weightings of the $n$ components summing to $n$. We address the problem of Feller processes that are not naturally summable as a sample from the resulting combinted distribution, and show that samples can be efficiently obtained using the acceptance-rejection algorithm. Of theoretical and practical importance, the combination distribution derived for the sum of squared independent gamma variables (a standard example) is a particular instance of the generalized approach applied to the sum of $n$ gamma variables; this yields a novel identity regarding the marginal distribution of such a sum. We demonstrate that the standard Gamma distribution and the Bessel K distribution both fall under the generalized framework. We also demonstrate that the Bessel K distribution is a building block for the Bayesian Lasso and Bayesian Bridge models. We also show that Bayesian methods for Feller processes are applicable to the Bayesian mixture of experts, Bayesian group Laplace, Bayesian group Lasso, Bayesian group exponential, Bayesian group inverse Gaussian, Bayesian group t, Bayesian group Cauchy, Bayesian group normal, Bayesian group uniform, Bayesian group exponential, Bayesian group inverse Gaussian, Bayesian group t, Bayesian group Cauchy, Bayesian group normal, Bayesian group uniform methods.

We introduce a consistent set of "Diagrammatic" equations designed to calculate the full wavefunction of collective multi-photon scattering events in waveguide quantum electrodynamics (QED) involving multi-excitation inputs. The "jump-Schrodinger" framework serves as the basis for our equations, which describe the system's quantum state evolution as a function of the photon propagation distance $z$. By utilizing these equations, we derived the "Fock-space" T-matrix elements required to determine exact amplitudes for any $N$-photon configuration in many-body quantum systems. To demonstrate their utility, we applied the method to multi-photon scattering scenarios in a two-site many-body system, showing how the equations facilitate the calculation of joint probabilities for multi-photon outcomes. Additionally, we outline a set of L-S coupling adaptation rules that enable the derivation of the system's effective Hamiltonian directly from the diagrammatic equations.

This research investigates enhanced dark matter (DM) distributions that arise when the initial DM density is significantly higher than the current cosmological average, potentially due to production mechanisms within the early universe. We introduce a spin-dependent dark matter-nucleus interaction model featuring a dimension-5 operator, coupled with the analysis of how initial DM density scales with the local DMS flux and cross-sections. Using hydrodynamic framework simulations, we determine the evolution of local DM density and its resulting flux and scattering rates, focusing on scenarios where the initial DM concentration is elevated. We identify that spin-dependent enhanced dark matter scenarios are more efficient at generating detectable signals than other models, particularly when the initial DM density is around 100 times the present cosmological value. Our findings indicate that the most promising experimental approaches involve direct detection experiments, direct detection of annihilation, and indirect detection methods.

Value-based approaches are fundamental to the successful deployment of reinforcement learning (RL) in real-world scenarios. However, designing effective hand-crafted rewards often proves difficult for non-experts, leading to suboptimal agent behaviors. This paper introduces a cluster ranking-based reward learning (RLRL) framework enhanced with a visual exploration agent. This concept was tested on two complex tasks involving environmental changes and dynamic, partially observable scenarios. In both cases, the proposed RLRL method allowed users to derive reward functions based on image-level labels, resulting in high-performance policies established with minimal manual effort.

That work established the existence of a metallic phase for bandwidths scaling as $W \sim N^{1/3}$, which this research expands upon by proving, under the same scaling conditions, an additional metallic regime for $N^{1/5} \lesssim W \lesssim N^{1/3}$. We achieve these results by approximating the finite-rank perturbations inherent in random band matrices with complex alterations of the sigma-model. By employing estimation techniques analogous to those in [arXiv:1504.08083], we demonstrate that Chiral Gaussian Unitary Ensemble (ChGUE) correlations govern random band matrices in this newly proven metallic region.

While pre-trained models have significantly advanced various natural language processing (NLP) areas, a notable gap remains in developing large-scale language models (LLMs) for comprehensive conversational understanding. In this study, we introduce a novel pre-training approach centered on converting conversational contexts into interpretable meaning representations. Specifically, we train an LLM to predict the semantic significance of individual turns within a chat session by distilling those meanings from a specialized meaning extractor. To facilitate this, we introduce a semantic graph representation that leverages structure to convey logical relationships and inherent ambiguities between human and machine speakers. Empirical results demonstrate that the resulting Meaning-of-Meaning Model (MMM) achieves superior performance compared to existing conversational LLMs across multiple tasks, including machine translation, machine comprehension, and machine conversation.

Algorithms are ubiquitous in daily life, yet their widespread adoption is hindered by a lack of trust in automated decisions. This paper introduces a novel framework for evaluating interpretability from the perspective of a human learner, contrasting it with existing approaches that are typically model-centric. We establish a formal definition of learnability, derive key properties, and subsequently distinguish between two categories: intrinsically interpretable and extrinisicallty interpretable models. Focusing on learners, our methodology involves a self-reported confidence metric alongside cognitive complexity. While model-independent for comparing cognitive complexity, various methods exist; we evaluate two such techniques and validate them empirically using both intriniscic and representative extrinsic model types. Our findings confirm that these measures effectively mirror the underlying theoretical distinctions in interpretability.

Anomaly detection operates under the unsupervised paradigm, a setting where no prior information about data is available, necessitating algorithms capable of identifying irregularities without relying on predefined labels. This work introduces TiWS-iForest, a lightweight, low-compute variant of the traditional Isolation Forest. Originally, the classic iForest required significant computational resources for both training and inference, which is prohibitive for edge and embedded systems. In contrast, TiWS-iForest achieves its name by integrating three key modifications: it is low-computation, operates within a tiny model footprint, and utilizes a loosely supervised approach. These factors collectively reduce memory consumption and processing time. Empirical evaluations on both synthetic and real-world datasets confirm that TiWS-iForest matches the performance of the full-precision Isolation Forest, all while delivering substantial savings in computational and memory resources.

This study proposes a new class of distributions that can be reparametrized using a Poisson process, a structure that facilitates the application of Bayesian inference for estimating extreme values. Specifically, we introduce a novel model named the shifted inverse square distribution (SIQD). The results demonstrate that the Bayesian estimator derived from Poisson-based data consistently outperforms the maximum likelihood estimator across various scenarios. Furthermore, we rigorously prove the asymptotic normality of the Bayes estimator and provide an explicit formula for its asymptotic variance.

This paper introduces a novel architecture for a common sense knowledge graph that integrates both symbolic and neural representations. The model utilizes a knowledge graph embedding approach employing knowledge distillation to train a neural node classifier, thereby enabling end-to-end reasoning. The architecture employs an attentional mechanism to dynamically select the most relevant subgraph for inference. Empirical results indicate that this model surpasses state-of-the-art performance on transductive tasks within the ATOMIC dataset, specifically in tasks involving instance retrieval and truth assessment. Additionally, a study examining the robustness of the model to noisy data reveals that while the system is susceptible to corrupt instances, its overall performance remains stable.

The Hi-GAL survey is designed to be the most comprehensive investigation of cold and warm molecular material within our Galaxy, targeting more than 10,000 infrared sources across four wavelength bands ranging from 4.5 to 850 $\mu$m. Capturing the necessary spectral coverage and spatial resolution demands a massive photon intake, which is processed by an advanced on-the-fly reduction pipeline. This system efficiently extracts scientific data from raw detector readings, generating both all-sky maps and catalogues containing individual source entries. Consequently, this pipeline serves as a vital component in maximizing the scientific potential of the Hi-GAL project.

The presence of NGC 2808's blue loops has long been explained by a mix of blue-straggler formation mechanisms, specifically stellar collisions and binary interactions, or by the evolution of helium-enriched Population III stars. We have previously calculated the precise age and metallicity of NGC 2808, determining an age of $10.0 \pm 0.2$ Gyr and a metallicity of $Z = 0.0196 \pm 0.0010$. These precise evolutionary tracks confirm that both the binary and population III interpretations are viable models for the observed blue loops.

This paper examines the steganography-based file-sharing platform, Cryptotex, and analyzes the duration statistics governing the initial exit times of files. The research demonstrates that, regardless of the underlying distribution, the cumulative exit-time function approximates a power law during its initial phase. Furthermore, while the standard deviation of these durations remains constant across different input distributions, the entropic power—the count of data points treated as hidden messages within exit-time records—exponentially increases as the StegDID detector runs for a growing number of files. Consequently, the entropic power serves as a highly sensitive metric for detecting Steganography in Synchromesh data, with the potential to identify hidden messages within relatively small datasets.

We propose an application of Bayesian inference to the observation of quantum systems. When the state of a system is represented as a positive operator, the reasoning behind updating beliefs regarding its measurement corresponds to applying the positive operator transform between probability distributions. Our analysis shows that the logical structure required to treat quantum measurement results as coherent with classical inference is met precisely when a specific positive operator—known as a quantum Bayes' theorem—exists. This operator generalizes the classical rule for probability revision to the quantum domain. Additionally, we demonstrate that the internal consistency of these updated beliefs is achieved if and only if the prior distribution and the positive operator describing the measurement are compatible (or commute). Our work confirms that the application of quantum Bayes' theorem is essential for modeling the consistent evolution of beliefs about quantum phenomena.

The JWST Fine Guidance Sensors (FGS) are designed to provide precise astrometry and high-contrast photometry for space-based observatories, including the Nancy Grace Roman Telescope's Wide-Field Infrared Surveyor (RITS-WFI) and the Roman High-Resolution Spectrograph (HRS). However, Earth's opaque Lyman-ultraviolet (UV) range (80–91 nm) hinders JWST and Roman from reaching their full potential in these areas. To overcome this limitation, a Lyman-alpha Screen (LAS) has been proposed to collect and redirect UV photons from space telescopes to a dedicated detector. This paper introduces the LAS prototype, a device engineered to precisely measure photon flux and particle count across a specific wavelength band. The prototype's performance is validated using a rigorous simulation framework that models its geometric structure, optical properties, and mechanical behavior.

This paper introduces a distributed solution to the network symmet breaking issue by utilizing local computational elements termed "graph devices." These autonomous devices interact solely with their immediate neighbors to collaboratively pinpoint symmetry-inducing breakers across the entire graph in a fully distributed manner. Each graph device is tasked with approximating the principal eigenpair of the associated symmetry matrix, a process facilitated by the standard distributed Lanczos algorithm deployed across all graph devices to achieve global convergence. The efficacy of this strategy stems from the graph symmetry, which ensures rapid convergence to a symmetrically relevant eigenpair through the Lanczos approach. Furthermore, to guarantee the convergence results presented herein, this work establishes a specific upper limit on communication delays within the framework.

Image cataloging is a well-established field in both industry and academia, with most current systems utilizing a two-stage workflow: first organizing images into clusters, then assigning descriptive tags to each cluster. This signature set represents the typical content found within an image group. However, this traditional pipeline encounters significant limitations when dealing with massive image collections. It requires a separate training phase for the content-based retrieval system and often produces tags that are not sufficiently granular. To overcome these hurdles, we introduce an untrained, unified framework capable of generating high-precision labels at multiple levels of granularity. This system seamlessly integrates scalable techniques for efficient image retrieval with advanced techniques for fine-grained content-based cataloging.

This paper investigates keyless physical layer identification and secure communication within AWGN environments. We present Keyless Verification (KLV), a novel framework that enables a transmitter to authenticate its received signal using a short, pre-shared secret key, without relying on a long channel. Under this approach, the transmitter sends a codeword from an unstructured, high-entropy distribution; the receiver generates an estimate of the transmitted sequence and sends its corresponding decision back to the transmitter. The transmitter then verifies the receiver's feedback to determine if the user is legitimate. We analyze the receiver's error probability and the secrecy capacity of KLV, demonstrating that the former converges exponentially to zero, while the former achieves a non-zero rate limit. We also show that the asymptotic error probability can be minimized by selecting codewords drawn from an unstructured distribution rather than a deterministic one.

This work examines the dispersion-free nature of transport observed in particles within weakly noisy, weakly inclined periodic arrays, focusing on regimes where the transport coefficient scales linearly with temperature. We demonstrate that this dispersion-free movement persists across the full spectrum of tilting forces and occurs in both the static and time-varying (fluctuating force) force scenarios. Additionally, we investigate the impact of particle asymmetry and correlation on the transport coefficient. Finally, we outline a strategy to compute the transport coefficient efficiently, even in complex systems comprising a large number of correlated particles.

Load balancing is essential for the efficient operation of contemporary cloud infrastructure. In this paper, we present Prepartioning, a novel method designed to improve the load balancing of virtual machine (VM) placement within a cloud environment. The proposed algorithm operates by first aggregating historical data regarding VM resource consumption and server hardware specifications to construct detailed usage profiles. These profiles are then utilized to generate an optimal VM-to-server assignment strategy aimed at minimizing the server activation count. Subsequent to the initial assignment, a real-time distribution phase continuously monitors active server loads and redistributes them to achieve optimal load balancing. Experimental evaluation demonstrates that the pre-deployment phase consistently selects the minimum necessary number of servers, while also delivering superior performance in maintaining balanced loads.

In large-scale networks of interacting agents, such as those in economic systems, the equilibrium state is often the primary focus. While game-theoretic frameworks are standard for analyzing these states, they require solving for a Nash equilibrium, a process that is often computationally prohibitive and may yield multiple, ambiguous outcomes. Consequently, there is an emerging need to forecast these equilibria directly from prior historical data. This paper introduces the Fixed Point Network (FPN), a neural architecture designed to forecast the collective outcomes of a variety of network games. The FPN is trained on an extensive collection of past games to generalize and predict the state of unseen games, performing effectively even when the number of participants is larger than any encountered during training.

This work investigates the asymptotic behavior of estimated causal impacts from the Lin et al. (2019) framework under the condition that the underlying model is misspecified. The analysis demonstrates that the estimator remains asymptotically normal, even in the absence of strong assumptions regarding conditional difference in differences. Unlike previous studies, we examine a high-dimensional setting where the number of control units may exceed the number of treatments. Furthermore, we derive the limiting distribution for applications involving the average treatment effect of interest, showcasing how a causal impact diverges significantly from a simple linear combination of treatment effects across control units. Simulations validate the methodological approach and reveal that the procedure yields accurate estimates of the average treatment effect without relying on heavy assumptions or tuning parameters.

This study addresses the anomaly detection challenge within linear time-invariant systems subjected to covert attacks. In this context, adversaries infiltrate specific sensors to compromise reading data, enabling the implementation of attack-induced anomalies. The proposed approach utilizes a two-stage framework: first, an effective system is derived from compromised data utilizing kernel-based learning techniques. Second, this learned effective system supports a Markov process for monitoring the system state and identifying anomalies. The effectiveness of the approach is validated through numerical examples demonstrating the method's ability to identify covert attacks.

This study proposes GAE-ISumm, a novel unsupervised framework designed for summarizing Indian language videos. It addresses the limitations of existing video summarization systems, which typically struggle with the linguistic and cultural complexities of non-English languages and Indian contexts specifically. Drawing on the assumption that significant segments of Indian videos focus on action, the system employs a unified architecture capable of extracting both the acoustic and visual components necessary for generating meaningful summaries. The methodology involves two key stages: initially, action is detected by segmenting action-rich video parts, and subsequently, action descriptions are extracted from both the relevant audio and visual data. Experimental results demonstrate that the system surpasses state-of-the-art English summarization baselines, thereby validating its effectiveness and potential for overcoming the barriers associated with Indian language media.

Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) are generative models that learn a latent representation $Z$ from observed data $X$ by approximating the posterior distribution $Q(Z|X)$ against the true posterior $P(Z|X)$. In VAEs, the Elbo loss is composed of two parts: the KL divergence between the posterior approximation and the prior, minus the reconstruction likelihood likelihood, i.e., $-\text{Evidence} \approx -\mathbb{D}_{KL} (Q || P) $ + \mathbb{L}_{Recon}$. In this work, we introduce a constrained VAE framework where the latent space $Q$ is restricted to a compact set $\Omega$. The optimization problem seeks the optimal $Q$ that minimizes the sum of the Elbo loss and a regularization term $\lambda g(Q)$: $\min_{Q} \mathbb{L}_{Elbo} + \lambda g(Q)$, where $g(Q)$ is a convex function and $\lambda > 0$ balances the trade-off between model fit and regularization. We propose a dual-based solver capable of handling arbitrary convex constraints efficiently. Theoretically, we prove dual feasibility and demonstrate dual convergence, showing that the primal objective values converge to their respective optima. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that our method outperforms non-constrained VAEs in producing tighter posterior approximations, leading to better reconstruction accuracy and lower posterior entropy.

The rapid adoption of IoT smart devices has resulted in significant energy consumption, prompting the need for intelligent management systems. This study introduces a novel architecture designed to facilitate effective control and monitoring of household appliances. The proposed system leverages IoT sensors for connectivity, integrates a private blockchain network to ensure secure communication, and utilizes IoT positioning technology to track device locations in real time. The main objective is to empower users with detailed insights into both their usage patterns and current locations, thereby promoting energy-efficient operation. The effectiveness of this framework was validated through extensive simulations and comparative evaluations against an existing public blockchain-based solution. Empirical results indicate that the private blockchain integration delivers superior performance in terms of transaction processing speed, security, storage efficiency, and overall reliability.

We introduce a novel deep learning-based deep learning framework designed to optimize the quantization of L-values in soft-decoding processes. Traditional methods rely on uniform quantization grids, which often result in suboptimal performance; our approach utilizes a neural network to generate non-uniform grids tailored to the specific characteristics of received signals. Additionally, we present a refined encoding strategy that replaces standard Gray-coded non-uniform quantization with one implemented through a deep learning model. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that the resulting L-value quantization and deep learning-encoded methods deliver superior bit-error-rate (BER) performance compared to both traditional uniform quantization and conventional Gray-coded schemes.

This study addresses the fundamental issue of determining whether a directed acyclic graph possesses an upward planar drawing. While this problem remains NP-complete for directed acyclic graphs with fixed maximum degree 3, it admits an efficient linear-time resolution under this constraint if either the quantity of edges or the maximum size of an antichain is restricted. By leveraging Buchsbaum, Pash, and others' findings on partial permutations, we demonstrate that any degree 3 directed acyclic graph with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges is upward planar provided a specific combinatorial condition holds. Furthermore, combining these results with techniques from Di Giacomo et al., we prove that every degree 3 directed acyclic graph containing at most $n - 2.25n^{5/3}$ edges satisfies upward planarity. Regarding the maximum chain size constraint, we show that if a directed acyclic graph has a maximum chain size of $n - O(\sqrt{n \log n})$, upward planarity can be checked efficiently. Finally, we establish that finding a maximum independent set in planar partial permutation graphs is NP-hard, even when restricted to those with a maximum chain size of 3.

Crowdsourcing has emerged as a cost-effective method for acquiring data and labels, yet it introduces significant challenges regarding data quality. In this paper, we introduce an uncertainty modeling framework designed to address the specific characteristics of noisy, crowdsourced information. Our approach employs an ensemble of neural network architectures—including a vanilla Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), and a ResNet—to analyze image datasets derived from the CrowdFlower Amazon Fashion Benchmark. By generating entropy distributions, referred to as "human softmax" distributions, we capture the variability in individual annotator judgments. Furthermore, specific metrics are developed to quantify and model the entropy inherent to annotator behavior. Our findings indicate that training on uncurated crowd data is feasible and that annotant diversity serves as a valuable indicator of uncertainty.

Directed evolutionary algorithms (DEAs) represent a specialized class of optimization methods designed to act as tools for the targeted exploration and synthesis of failure modes within systems. The objective of a DEA is to systematically identify and reproduce specific, pre-defined faults in a given device under test by evolving test sequences that trigger these failures; notably, the algorithm leverages user-provided feedback regarding the proximity of a generated test to activating the target failure. This research details a contribution to the D-EA community through the development of a directed algorithm that replicates stuck-at faults in combinational logic circuits. Our approach employs a genetic algorithm driven by a fitness function grounded in the distance to the target fault, utilizing an objective function based on the Hamming distance of input vectors to the fault-inducing condition. We validated this approach through an experiment involving the reproduction of multiple stuck-at faults across several digital circuits, with visualization of results performed using SPICE simulations. Empirical results demonstrate that the algorithm successfully successfully reproduced all targeted stuck-at faults in the tested circuits, thereby confirming the viability of this method for this application. Furthermore, this study constitutes the initial known attempt to apply a directed algorithm specifically to the task of failed-stuck-at-fault reproduction.

In high-$T_c$ cuprate superconductors, vortex dynamics are complicated by interactions among vortices, flux lines, and the anisotropic superconducting gap. To address this, we performed high-resolution muon spin relaxation and precession studies on Bi$_{2-x}$Y$_x$Sr$_2$CuO$_{6+\delta}$ across diverse magnetic fields and temperatures to examine vortex evolution. Our data indicate that at low doping levels ($x=0.15$), the vortex lattice undergoes a transition from hexagonal to quadrupolar symmetry near the melting point as the field increases. This behavior signals the emergence of a vortex grid with square symmetry at higher fields, coexisting with a hexagonal single-vortex grid at lower fields. We attribute this square symmetry to strong vortex-vortex interactions and suggest it results from the annihilation of antivortices located within the superconducting nodal gaps. This finding provides the first direct experimental confirmation of such a grid transition in a cuprate family superconductor.

Our premise rests on the insight that the shear-to-baryon-pressure ratio ($\eta/s$) significantly shapes the thermal photon angular flow pattern. Consequently, the flow vector, angle, and width of these distributions function as indicators of QGP viscosity. To substantiate this, we performed a Bayesian analysis of both flow vector and angle data from PHENIX and STAR collaborations regarding central Au+Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}=200$ GeV. This framework simultaneously incorporates thermal photon data alongside flow vectors, angles, and widths, while accounting for contributions from thermal quark-gluon plasma photons, jet photons, and thermal hadron photons. Our results demonstrate that the QGP viscosity range is well-constrained by including the photon flow patterns, specifically narrowing from the prior bounds of $0.04\leq (\eta/s)_{\rm QGP}\leq 0.12$ to $0.04\leq (\eta/s)_{\rm QGP}\leq 0.08$.

While prior research has extensively analyzed this phenomenon in isolated, short exchanges involving unacquainted speakers, it remains poorly understood within the broader context of extended dialogues involving groups. This study introduces an unmonitored metric for calculating an entrainment distance that quantifies the alignment of speech rates among multiple participants. The proposed method employs deep neural networks to automatically detect these distances from raw audio, eliminating the need for painstaking and expensive manual acoustic analyses. Additionally, the researchers investigate how these computed entrainment distances shift throughout various phases of a conversation, offering the first empirical account of the evolution of an entrainment "metric curve" within natural, unrestricted dialogues.

We introduce the release of www.rcsed.org, an open-access platform featuring instruments to visualize spectral and imaging data. Designed for the analysis of time-series observations from the Rapid Broadband Survey of the Extended Galactic Center (Rapid Broadband Survey of the Extended Galactic Center Survey Data Archive / RCSEDv2), this site integrates three primary features: a data archive holding the survey records, an interactive map for spatial exploration, and tools for spectral examination. To facilitate broader scientific use, these tools are built upon the Spectral Explorer and the Multi-wavelength Map visualization libraries, both of which remain accessible as standalone resources. We detail the specific functionalities offered by this platform and describe the ongoing efforts to expand its capabilities.

This work addresses the challenge of Temporal Action Division (TAD), a task that involves segmenting a video into atomic actions based on user text descriptions. Since action labels are rarely available for most video datasets, we introduce SSCAP: a Self-Supervised Co-occurrence Activity Parsing approach that enables unsupervised discovery of temporal actions without requiring any annotated supervision. Unlike many other methods, SSCAP does not rely on pre-training with external datasets or fine-tuning with specific datasets. Instead, SSCAP learns to parse video content by analyzing the co-occurrence patterns of temporal action parts. Empirical results demonstrate that SSCAP achieves superior performance compared to other unsupervised methods and maintains competitive results against supervised approaches on the TAD task. Additionally, the code and models will be made open-source at \url{https://github.com/zhenguo123/SSCAP}.

This study examines concealed-charm pentaquark states, specifically focusing on the now-established $P_c(4312)$ and $P_c(4440)$ resonances observed by the LHCb collaboration within $\Lambda_b^0$ baryon decays to $J/\psi\Lambda_b^0$. While these decays inherently involve quark-antiquark pair creations and $Q\bar{Q}$ annihilations, we employ $Q^c$ algebra to analyze both processes. Our analysis indicates that the $c\bar{c}$ components of the resulting pentaquarks are predominantly arranged in a spin configuration of $S_{c\bar{c}}=1$. Our results demonstrate that these creation amplitudes are generally an order of magnitude greater than the corresponding annihilation amplitudes.

This study explores testing education concepts using an empirical approach. It introduces a new, inquiry-based testing pedagogy that employs compact, conceptual questions to guide students toward self-discovered principles. The research evaluates the efficacy of this teaching method through a randomized controlled trial. The study offers two distinct arms for comparison: a conventional detailed-feedback approach versus the novel inquiry-based conceptual-feedback approach designed to foster questions thinking. The findings indicate that students in the new approach demonstrated significantly superior performance on both conceptual and practical testing tasks compared to those relying on traditional feedback, thereby supporting its adoption as a superior methodology in testing education.

Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (UDA) is essential for practical domain adaptation, particularly when target label information is unavailable. While existing methods typically require access to source training data, this constraint limits their usability in specific scenarios. This paper introduces a novel theoretical approach to transfer concepts from a training dataset to facilitate domain adaptation, effectively eliminating the reliance on target label data. By mathematically analyzing the implications of this transfer, we demonstrate that an optimal theoretical framework can be achieved by transferring an appropriate kernel operator. Leveraging this insight, we introduce a semi-supervised Transfer Target Transfer (sUDDA) model that reduces adaptation costs by integrating labeled and unlabeled information to align the kernel operators of source and target domains through the application of entropic regularizations to keep regularization complexity under control. Extensive experiments across various source-to-target scenarios, including Office-31, Office-12, and Tesla, demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance. Furthermore, theoretical insights and empirical evaluations confirm that our method is robust to shifts in data distribution even when training data is scarce or insufficient.

Gas-core reactors (GCRs) are proposed as a power source for deep space missions, utilizing a plasma fuel that remains in a disordered, gaseous state above its critical point despite intense neutron flux. This document reviews the GCR concept, emphasizing the scientific and engineering hurdles that require further research and development. We argue that GCRs hold significant promise as both propulsion power sources and electrical generators for distant spacecraft. This analysis begins by establishing the fundamental GCR design parameters, such as the necessary power density, net power output, and overall size. We then outline the essential physical principles governing their operation, focusing on how plasma stability is maintained in a nuclear critical mass. Additionally, this text details the envisioned GCR configuration, focusing on the reactor assembly, its cooling mechanisms, and associated systems. We also explore potential pathways for constructing a functional GCR by leveraging existing gas-plasma research and advanced nuclear reactor technologies. Finally, we outline a comprehensive roadmap for future mission planning, including necessary steps such as conceptual designs, proof-of-concept demonstrations, and full-scale development.

Locating particle interactions in particle detectors is a critical function for modern experimental astrophysics, particularly within the context of neutrino research. Although current neural network approaches have achieved superior performance over traditional algorithms, they remain confined to narrowly defined, pre-labeled datasets. Our study presents two innovations to resolve these issues: a transferable neural design and a deterministic algorithm. Our findings indicate that while transferable networks facilitate the adaptation to new, out-of-distribution scenarios through fine-tuning, the deterministic approach enables the reuse of shared labeling efforts across experiments.

Atmospheric models for cool brown dwarfs and exoplanets are hindered by the computational cost of repeatedly running line-by-by line radiative transfer calculations. To overcome this, researchers often employ lookup tables (LUTs) that store pre-computed absorption cross-sections, though generating these collections is both computationally intensive and hindered by varied coding practices. To resolve these issues, we introduce EXOPLINES: a public repository (https://exoline.sai.msu.ru/) that provides absorption cross-sections optimized for brown dwarfs and giant exoplanets, covering a temperature range of 500–3000 K and pressures from 0.01 to 1000 bar. This collection includes 15 molecular species representing 1600 spectra, spanning wavelengths from 0.3 to 250 μm. Exoline significantly streamlines forward modeling workflows for brown dwarf and exoplanet atmospheres, eliminating the need to generate spectra on the fly and thereby avoiding the pitfalls associated with diverse, inconsistent code implementations.

This work investigates two-dimensional higher-order topological insulators (HOTIs) affected by disorder, specifically examining the impact of different boundary conditions on their bulk-boundary correspondence. By focusing on models with varying masses at corners and edges, we observe that while bulk spectral statistics remain consistent across conditions, the emergence of higher- and lower-order edge and corner modes follows distinct mass-dependent patterns. Specifically, we define mass bounds that, together with topological invariants, completely characterize these one-dimensional modes, establishing mass-bound correspondences for mass transitions that bulk topology does not capture. We also introduce an order-specific invariant set that establishes the limits of this correspondence. Ultimately, these findings demonstrate that bulk-boundary correspondence must be expanded to include mass bounds, evolving into a mass-bound boundary correspondence within the framework of disordered systems.

This study provides an overview of the LHC and CMS experiment's efforts in investigating parameters within SUSY models. The discussion leverages results from both simplified and comprehensive scenarios. We present a new approach for high-quality, real-time view synthesis of brightness fields, which model direct illumination across scenes. While rendering noise-free images at high resolutions, brightness fields struggle with indirect lighting and exhibit poor performance at near viewpoints. To leverage their strengths, we introduce a renderer that integrates a neural radiance cache, enabling fast sampling of existing view directions and significantly reducing the need for ray tracing. Additionally, we develop a neural adapter that synthesizes colors for novel directions, filling the gaps left by the cache. Our method produces renderings that are visually comparable to radiance fields, outperform traditional ray tracing, and achieves speeds of up to 100 fps on a single GPU.

This report details the 2020 operational performance of the speckle interferometry program at the Southern Astrophysical Research (SOAR) telescope, along with the identified scientific results.
