This paper introduces a new text classification approach to address the limitations of conventional methods, which often rely on complex models that struggle to adapt to evolving threats and demand extensive training data. We propose a lightweight, conceptually straightforward method designed to identify underperforming classifiers and instantly deploy more suitable models in response to emerging attacks. The core of this approach involves modifying existing models by integrating underperforming features into a weighted ensemble, utilizing Sibuya variants to dynamically adjust classification. We detail the operational logic of these Sibuya variants and detail an implementation of the method for ridge regression-based text classification. Experimental results demonstrate that this robust, low-complexity technique effectively counters label-flipping attacks, achieving accuracy levels superior to those of a pre-trained model.

This work introduces a novel approach to automatically generate 3D models based on a single 2D image, specifically targeting the domain of linear architectural drawings. These designs rely on a strict geometry where walls are represented as straight segments that intersect at 90-degree angles, and interior spaces are depicted as polygons. We present an optimized methodology to automatically convert the 2D input into a 3D model by integrating the known constraints and modeling assumptions inherent to linear architectural depictions. By formulating the single-view scene reconstruction problem as a probabilistic graphical model, we derive a closed-form solution using the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm to maximize a convex likelihood function derived from a Gaussian distribution. We evaluate our approach on both synthetic data and real-world images, demonstrating that it successfully generates high-fidelity 3D models that accurately reflect the original design.

Neural machine translation (NMT) models are often resource-intensive, prompting the use of knowledge distillation and quantization to deploy smaller, resource-efficient alternatives. However, these techniques carry the risk of degrading translation quality. This study evaluates their robustness in low-resource languages by investigating how well smaller NMT models generalize to languages with limited data. Using a case study on sign language translation, we assess translation performance across three scenarios: seeing only a low-resource target language during training, restricting the training to a single parallel corpus, and utilizing a weak teacher model. Results indicate that while both techniques can maintain translation quality and enable model compression, they are surprisingly fragile when training conditions change, leading to significant performance drops.

Although advanced vision-language models (VLMs) have achieved significant success in numerous applications, their generated descriptions frequently fail to align with end-users' specific needs or intended meanings. Addressing this gap, we introduce a novel framework called Mediated Descriptions for Intention Alignment (MiDiA). The proposed method maintains the original image while inserting an intermediate layer that adapts the generated descriptions to better match the user's intent. Crucially, this mediation step does not require retraining or fine-tuning the pre-trained VLM, nor does it necessitate any extra inputs beyond standard image-image pairs or specific description elements. Instead, we employ a training-free prompting strategy that leverages the model's inherent capabilities to ensure intention alignment. Empirical results demonstrate that our approach achieves higher alignment scores than strong baseline methods and remains effective even when applied within VLM architectures that have not been explicitly optimized for generating textual descriptions.

We introduce a formal definition for an intuitive, broad concept of "intended damage," applicable to diverse settings and without relying on a specific formalism. Additionally, we propose a general definition of intendedness that functions independently of any particular framework for identifying intended damage.

Deep learning has emerged as a highly effective technique for addressing complex challenges across various domains. However, constructing and deploying deep neural networks often demands specialized knowledge and experience, particularly when requiring continuous adaptation to new data or expansion into novel network architectures. To address these limitations, scholars and industry experts have introduced MMLSpark, a deep learning framework integrated within the MLSpark ecosystem, which offers user-friendly interfaces for modifying and enlarging existing models and networks. By enabling seamless application to fresh data sources and smooth integration into new network structures, MMLSpark facilitates straightforward deployment of deep learning solutions on real-world infrastructure via cloud platforms.

Voice interpretation involves using a speaker's utterances to transmit information to a listener. In this study, we explore the concept of "zero-shot" interpretation, where a speaker and listener have never encountered each other's acoustic characteristics prior to communication. To address this, we introduce a "neural speaker normalization" method, which maps unknown voices to a standard reference using noise normalization as a foundational reference. Experiments were conducted in a cross-dialect setting with Arabic as the language. The findings reveal that while noise normalization provides a baseline, our zero-shot interpretation system further enhances performance by anchoring to a neutral, reference-agnostic style. Specifically, our method achieves a 10.5% increase in the average mutual information rate between speaker and listener compared to standard noise normalization.

A novel methodology for estimating daily peak demands within the low-voltage grid is introduced, utilizing daily maximum values to enhance the accuracy of peak load forecasts. This approach involves integrating day-ahead forecasts derived from probabilistic load data across several distributions, specifically the normal, log-normal, and Weibull. Additionally, the model incorporates the distribution of daily historical maxima to refine predictions. The study evaluates model performance using real-world data from Germany, comparing it against a baseline that relies exclusively on the recorded maximum values. The results indicate that the proposed method significantly outperforms the traditional approach, reducing the root mean square error (RMSE) by 10.2% on average, while also achieving a 10.2% reduction in the RMSE for the peak load specifically.

We introduce a structured framework for embedding domain expertise within machine learning (ML) initiatives. Recognizing that a vast and rapidly evolving body of knowledge surrounds every ML application, yet current standard operating procedures lack clear guidelines on how to leverage such expertise effectively, our work offers a foundational blueprint. We outline the essential steps to systematically incorporate these insights into a domain-specific ML project, a process that enhances model performance, boosts stakeholder trust, and ultimately delivers superior outcomes.

Recent studies utilizing deep learning for lesion localization and segmentation in dermatology frequently rely on dense classification, an approach known to be expensive and impractical for clinical settings. In this paper, we introduce a dataset of 1,000 images featuring 2,200 anonymized, geolocated lesions collected globally to assess model impartiality. Using this new resource, we demonstrate the effectiveness of a weakly supervised method for task-specific impartial learning via geometric segmentation, which achieves competitive results against dense classifiers without sacrificing accuracy. Specifically, this approach achieves an F1 score of 0.62 on the new benchmark (surpassing prior state-of-the-art methods) while incurring only 4% performance degradation. Furthermore, the method demonstrates superior generalization on external benchmarks like ISIC 2019 and ISIC 2020, achieving improvement gains of 5% and 8%, respectively.

Accurately positioning and identifying vertebrae in computed tomography (CT) scans is essential for diagnosing and treating various spinal diseases. However, achieving this is difficult due to significant variations in scan and X-ray parameters, patient anatomy, and imaging artifacts. These inconsistencies often render automated localization and recognition systems ineffective. This study introduces a robust method for vertebrae localization and recognition that leverages deep learning, grounded in two key contributions: a vertebrae atlas and a vertebrae-aware enhancement network. First, to address spinal irregularities and artifacts, we introduce a newly vertebrae-aware regularization algorithm that adapts scanning protocols to produce consistent CT scans, thereby enabling precise localization and recognition. Second, we develop a convolutional neural network (CNN) that incorporates anatomical knowledge to further enhance recognition performance. Experimental evaluations across three datasets yielded a vertebrae positioning accuracy of 98.6% and a recognition success rate of 96.8%.

We present a theoretical model for the dynamical stabilization of a high-energy electron within a vacuum cavity subjected to an intense oscillating electromagnetic field. The analysis demonstrates that resonant electrons are uniquely and robustly protected from complete disintegration into lower-energy states. The study further reveals a novel scaling law for the electron-maser interaction under the influence of parameter dressing effects. Additionally, we provide a phenomenological framework to explain resonant electron dynamics in regimes of extreme light-matter coupling.

While electric actuators are standard in legged robots, integrating elastic components presents significant manufacturing and maintenance difficulties. To address this, the paper proposes a machine learning-driven method that automatically determines optimal elastic actuation profiles to enhance both the agility and durability of legged robots. Our approach involves generating a comprehensive dataset of robot trajectories and time-varying environment parameters alongside corresponding torque requirements for rigid configurations. A neural network is then trained to forecast torque for an elasticized quadruped based on these inputs. Our methodology is validated through high-fidelity simulation using Webots and a customized version of the MuJoCo physics engine. Experimental results indicate that the proposed policy effectively leverages elasticity to substantially boost performance and robustness against perturbations compared to a fully rigid baseline.

This study addresses the problem of divisibility in quantum mechanics by proposing a novel variational approach designed to calculate the minimal dimension $d$ associated with a given state. Central to this methodology is the construction of an auxiliary Hamiltonian that forces the state to reside within a subspace of dimension $d$. Through the implementation of a variational principle, the method computes the expectation value of this Hamiltonian. A key advantage lies in its flexibility: it can be applied to both Hermitian and non-Hermitian systems, allowing for the determination of the dimension $d$ for any given state. Consequently, the approach serves as a valuable resource for investigating divisibility properties and related quantum correlations.

Magnetic reconnection is central to numerous astrophysical phenomena, ranging from solar flares and coronal mass ejections to the dynamics of Earth's magnetosphere and active galactic nuclei. This study investigates the growth rate of tearing modes in slab geometries by examining a small-scale regime that lies between the classical and polytropic limits within collisionless plasmas. Drawing on collisional findings by R. M. Kulsrud and N. I. Barnes, our work demonstrates that in these collisionless environments, the recombination rate exhibits a linear dependence on the logarithm of the ratio between the l and the distance to the minimum of the m-function. Additionally, a novel analytical formula is derived to calculate the k-growth rate of these modes at the collisionless scale, and a comparative analysis is made with the polytrophic model. The proposed theory aligns with numerical simulations conducted by the A. B. Kulsrud group. This theory also offers insights into the physics of magnetic reconnection in collisionless plasillas, as well as potential applications in astrophysical settings where collisional effects are negligible.

Feature-based trait manipulation (TLT) is a recent approach designed to handle fashion image retrieval (FIR). The process involves two phases: first, modifying individual features of an image to align it with a specific user preference, and second, matching these altered versions against a database. While effective, current state-of-the-art methods are constrained to operating on low-resolution images of 64×64 pixels. This study introduces a novel TL-driven framework for FIR that functions at a higher resolution (256×256). The proposed method employs a multi-scale architecture utilizing both Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) and Transformer models to facilitate the manipulation and matching stages. Experimental results indicate a significant performance boost, achieving an improvement of 10% in Mean Average Precision (MAP) compared to the best existing solutions.

This study examines methods for resolving linear ill-posed equations within the framework of Banach spaces. Inspired by the classical Tikhonov approach, a dual gradient ascent algorithm is introduced; this algorithm seeks to identify a regularizing filter function that enhances the convergence rate of the solution. Utilizing a novel dual variational argument, a universal convergence rate is established, subsequently leading to the design of an optimized penalization term for Tikhonov that elevates the convergence rate to the optimal level. Two illustrative examples demonstrate how the proposed algorithms and the Tikhonov approach can significantly accelerate convergence rates.

Light field (LF) cameras offer the capability to post-capture adjust focal lengths and viewing angles, yet their fixed, compact sensor arrays result in low resolution and high pixel quantization errors, often causing unreliable depth estimation. This study introduces a novel technique to enhance depth quality by exploiting super-resolution through multiple offset views. By integrating these LF-derived depth maps, we develop an algorithm that identifies and mitigates artifacts arising from the chosen offset views. Consequently, this approach yields robust depth data even when dealing with challenging inputs such as specularities, missing data, and high-contrast edges. To facilitate this, we develop an OpenCV-compatible tool called Response to Offset Expenses (ReOCE) for generating offset views. This tool optimizes the offset view selection by analyzing view consistency, ensuring the final reconstructed depth maintains high quality, particularly in difficult regions.

We investigate non-Riemannian regimes of gravity that manifest when the standard metric is replaced by the scalar and vector degrees of freedom inherent in theafilatetrfield and its dual, known as the dual theory. In this context, the metric emerges dynamically rather than being fundamental. Specifically, the work focuses on the Florides-Wheeler framework, the dual of Horndeski gravity, and the dual of General Relativity. For each case, the corresponding field equations are derived, the relationship between these formulations and the standard metric is established, and the equations are solved to identify viable cosmological solutions. Finally, the relationship between these dualities is outlined to position non-Riemannian gravity within a broader unified hierarchy.

The proliferation of wireless devices has strained in-home Wi-Fi networks, causing significant user dissatisfaction. Addressing this, the Ieee 802.11 standard suite introduces mechanisms like 802.11k (neighbor AP selection), 802.11v (network management), and the new 802.11r (extender radio management) to enhance performance. This paper proposes a novel algorithm for router and range extender selection that lever the channel load information provided by the 802.11r protocol. The approach operates in two phases: first, utilizing the channel load data to identify the optimal AP with the least congested environment; second, applying the same logic to select the ideal range extender. The proposed method demonstrates superior performance compared to the existing Random Router Management (802.11r) protocol.
